beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer — the ask lands answered
beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on the physics engine, a tool that lets an A.I. solve physics problems without doing the math itself. Ask a chatbot a physics question and you get a confident number. But who actually computed it? Usually, the same model that wrote the sentence. This project splits that job in two.

props.command: Explain how the physics engine solves a physics problem, and who actually does the math.
output: The AI reads the problem and picks the formula
A symbolic solver does every calculation
When it can't solve something, it says so

beats.new_visual_element: executive summary — three things this video proves
beats.narration_text: Here's the plan. In about three minutes, you'll see three things. First, who does what: the language model reads, and a math library calculates. Second, how the engine decides, before solving, whether its answer can be trusted. And third, what the team has actually proven, and what they say is still unproven. You don't need any physics or coding background. Every term gets defined when it shows up.

beats.new_visual_element: words to the model, math to the solver
beats.narration_text: The answer, up front. A large language model, the kind of A.I. behind a chatbot, is great with words and unreliable at arithmetic. So in this engine, the model never does arithmetic or algebra. It reads the problem, picks the formula, and explains the result. Every calculation goes to SymPy, a library that does algebra exactly, the way you would on paper, plus pint, a library that tracks units. Words to the model. Math to the solver.

One thing to clear up. Physics engine usually means the code inside a video game that makes things fall and bounce. This is not that. It's a physics problem solving engine. A homework style question goes in, and a structured solution comes out: the answer, the formula it used, and every assumption it made. It's built as a tool that Medhavy, the learning platform it was designed for, can call whenever a student asks a physics question.

Every question moves through five steps. Parse turns the words into knowns, unknowns, and units. Retrieve pulls candidate formulas from a library of formula cards. A card is one formula, plus the conditions where it's allowed. Plan checks those conditions, and confirms the problem can actually be solved. If something's missing, it goes back for another card. Solve hands the equations to SymPy. And Verify checks the units, and where it can, solves the problem a second, independent way.

Here's the clever part. Before solving anything, the engine asks one question. How many formula cards fit this problem? If exactly one fits, the answer is final, and it comes out the same every time. If more than one fits, it doesn't quietly pick a favorite. It returns every candidate answer, and asks the A.I. to judge which formula matches the situation, not to redo the math. And if none fit, it says so, hands the problem to the A.I., and logs the gap, so someone can write a new card.

So does it work? The team's own checks report sixteen out of sixteen test problems correct, across mechanics and electricity and magnetism. One problem, run ten times in a row, gives exactly the same output, down to the last character. And on a classic pulley problem from the OpenStax physics textbook, the published answer is three point two seven meters per second squared. The engine returns three point two six six seven. Same answer, just not rounded.

Now the honest part, and the team wrote it down themselves. Parsing is unmeasured. The demo feeds in problems that were already parsed correctly. There's no baseline yet, so nobody has measured how a plain chatbot does on the same problems. Coverage is thin. Against one thousand two hundred twenty six real university physics problems, rigid body dynamics has one hundred eighty problems, and one card. And it isn't deployed. No student has used it yet.

beats.new_visual_element: three questions to ask any AI answer
beats.narration_text: So here's what you can take away. When an A.I. hands you a number, ask three questions. Who did the math, the model or a solver? Did anything check the units? And would it tell you if it didn't know? This engine answers all three by design, and writes its gaps down. The card library will grow, and these numbers will change. The rule won't. Words to the model. Math to the solver.

Your turn. Paste this prompt into Claude, along with a physics problem from your own class. It asks Claude to separate the reading from the calculating, check the units, and tell you which step it couldn't verify.

props.command: Here is a physics problem: [paste it]. First list the knowns, unknowns, and units. Then name the formula and when it applies. Then solve it with code, not mental math, check the units, and tell me which step you could not verify.
output: Solved in code · units checked · gaps named
